statement: In an international online survey of people who had drunk ayahuasca (2017 to 2019; 6,877 self-selected respondents who had drunk with no more than two groups; Perkins et al., 2021), the setting of their last ceremony, as they described and rated it looking back, was associated with how much extreme fear they recalled and with difficulties afterwards, by small amounts. Of the 6,817 with a known setting, 52.1% had last drunk in an ayahuasca church (87% of them living in Brazil, and more than half having drunk over 200 times), 19.6% with traditional shamans and 28.3% in other settings; in these last two groups about two in three had drunk five times or fewer. Adjusted for age, sex, education, number of mental-health diagnoses, times drunk, years since the last drink, the three motivation scores and the other ceremony and support variables, each point higher on a 1-to-4 rating of support and safety (averages 3.4 to 3.9) went with less extreme fear or panic (−0.29 on a 0-to-10 scale, SE 0.07) and fewer difficulties in the weeks after (−0.13, SE 0.05); each point higher on a rating of the preparation offered (a chance to discuss one's history and concerns, and guidance on difficulties, before drinking) went with fewer later difficulties (−0.14, SE 0.03) but showed no detectable association with fear (−0.01, SE 0.04, p = 0.82). More fear went with more traditional practices (0.18 per practice, of up to 6), with drinking mostly in Amazonian countries other than Brazil (0.7), with therapeutic reasons for drinking (0.21 per reason) and with mental-health diagnoses (0.21 per diagnosis); less fear went with church features such as hymns or sermons (−0.38) and with each decade of age (−0.22). Fasting, offered at 35% of traditional settings, 26% of other settings and 2% of churches, showed no detectable difference in fear (−0.07 points on the 0-to-10 scale, 95% CI −0.29 to 0.15), later difficulties (−0.05, −0.21 to 0.11) or current distress (Kessler-10 −0.28, −0.69 to 0.13; editors' intervals): no difference was detected, which is not the same as showing there is none, since the fear interval runs from 0.29 points lower to 0.15 points higher. Fasting went with slightly higher ratings of mystical experience (1.7 points on a 9-to-90 scale) and of growth in well-being. Across the whole range of either rating, current distress differed by under 2 points on the 40-point Kessler scale (editors' arithmetic). Ratings and outcomes were reported by the same people at one sitting, on average 1.2 to 1.6 years after their last drink; the fear question did not say which session it meant, while the ceremony ratings concerned the last one; nothing was measured before ayahuasca, the amount and content of the brew were not recorded, no average or spread is given for the fear and difficulty measures, and the authors note that the sample may lean towards people with good experiences. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one large survey, people who felt safe and supported at their last ayahuasca ceremony recalled a little less fear and fewer problems in the weeks after. Being offered a chance to talk things through beforehand went with fewer problems afterwards, but not with less fear, and fasting showed no detectable link with either. The same people rated the ceremony and their experience, looking back, and the differences were small.
population: People who have drunk ayahuasca, self-selected through ayahuasca organizations, retreat centres, churches and online groups (half of them church members, mostly in Brazil)
exposure: Features of the last ceremony as the respondents described and rated them: church, traditional-shaman or other setting; support and safety; preparation offered; traditional or religious practices; fasting; country where they mostly drank
comparator: Respondents who rated or described their last ceremony differently, adjusted for age, sex, education, mental-health diagnoses, times drunk and years since the last drink
outcome: Extreme fear or panic during a session (0 to 10), difficulties in the weeks or months after, mystical-experience and growth ratings, and current distress (Kessler-10)
magnitude: Adjusted B (SE): support and safety (per point, 1 to 4) extreme fear −0.29 (0.07), later difficulties −0.13 (0.05), Kessler-10 −0.62 (0.12); preparation offered (per point) later difficulties −0.14 (0.03), fear −0.01 (0.04, p = 0.82), Kessler-10 −0.25 (0.07); extreme fear: traditional practices 0.18 per practice, traditional country 0.7, therapeutic motivation 0.21, mental-health diagnoses 0.21, church features −0.38, age −0.22 per decade; fasting: fear −0.07 (0.11; 95% CI −0.29 to 0.15), later difficulties −0.05 (0.08; −0.21 to 0.11), Kessler-10 −0.28 (0.21; −0.69 to 0.13) (editors' intervals), mystical orientation 1.69 (0.64), growth 0.97 (0.37). Across a whole rating, under 2 Kessler-10 points (editors' arithmetic). The paper does not say which outcomes were modelled as ordinal; the fear coefficients are read as points on the 0-to-10 item, which assumes a linear model, and no mean or SD is given for the fear item or the difficulty count.

statement: In 2,561 adults who answered an anonymous online survey in 2018 after recruitment through websites and forums (for example reddit, dmt-nexus, bluelight and drugs-forum) and by email (mean age 31.9; 77% men; 85% White; 64% living in the USA; a median of 6 lifetime DMT uses), all of whom reported at least one encounter with a seemingly autonomous being or entity (the study's term) after a 'breakthrough' dose of DMT (defined as one with very strong effects), smoked or vaporized without other substances, and each describing their single most memorable encounter, on average about 4.6 years earlier (editors' calculation from the mean ages now and at the experience), the respondents reported the following (Davis et al., 2020). Only people who reported an encounter could take part, so the survey cannot show how often encounters happen; of the 9,179 eligible people who consented, 4,610 completed the survey and affirmed their answers, and 2,049 of these (editors' sum) were then excluded, by design (103 with a psychotic disorder diagnosis, 1,279 who had taken other substances that may have affected the experience, 457 who took DMT another way) or for duplicate addresses, undisclosed substance use, use of changa or inattentive answers (34 and 176). For 67% the encounter described was their first. They reported mainly seeing (92%) and extrasensory, for example telepathic, contact (85%); 84% reported communication with the entity, 40% two-way and 49% one-way from the entity, most often by telepathy (74%). From a list (all that apply), they called it a being (60%), guide (43%), spirit (39%), alien (39%), helper (34%), angel (16%), elf (14%), religious personage (11%), plant spirit (10%), fairy (8%), clown (6%), demon (6%) or deceased family member (2%), among other labels. During the encounter they felt joy (65%), trust (63%), surprise (61%), love (59%), kindness (56%), friendship (48%) and fear (41%); love was most often the single most prominent emotion (21%), fear for 7%, and 32% rated it, psychologically, among the five most challenging experiences of their lives. Rated moderately or more, the entity seemed conscious (96%), intelligent (96%), benevolent (78%) and sacred (70%), and malicious to 11%. Looking back from now, 65% judged the experience more real than everyday waking consciousness (81% as it felt at the time); 49% placed the entity in some real but different dimension or reality, 26% there and in everyday physical reality, 9% completely within themselves and 1% only in everyday reality; 72% believed it continued to exist after the encounter; and 80% said the experience altered their fundamental conception of reality (60% of all respondents called the change desirable, 1% undesirable). 69% (1,773) said they received a message, task, mission, purpose or insight, which the authors coded into themes, most often idiosyncratic information (703), personal insight (571) and love (409); 19% (484) said they received a prediction about the future, most often about a personal life event (156), which the authors call unverifiable with their method. Asked in the same sitting about their religious identification before the encounter and now, 28% recalled being atheist before and 10% said they were atheist now; agnostic 27% and 16%; a belief in ultimate reality, a higher power, God or universal divinity 36% and 58% (each change p < 0.001 by z-tests for paired proportions with Bonferroni correction; no cross-tabulation printed), so at least 64% of those who recalled being atheist no longer identified as atheist (editors' arithmetic; the abstract says more than half). Most attributed lasting positive changes to the experience, for example in well-being or life satisfaction (89%) and life's purpose (82%), and 1% to 5% negative changes, with nothing measured before the experience and no comparison group. The abstract concludes that the experience and how people interpreted it brought deep and lasting changes in their worldview, and the Discussion presents the survey as strong evidence of such changes, while the limitations say that the cross-sectional design 'makes causal interpretations impossible' and cannot show whether the sample represents people who use DMT; the authors add that harms may be underestimated, because people whose lives had been seriously disrupted by such an experience may have been less inclined to take part, and each person described only their most memorable experience. All of these are the respondents' reports and beliefs, not findings about whether such beings exist. The study was funded by a US National Institute on Drug Abuse training grant, the Heffter Research Institute and the Johns Hopkins Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research (itself funded by a private foundation and individual donors); the authors declared no conflicts of interest. A separate, earlier online survey by the same Johns Hopkins group (Griffiths et al., 2019), whose questionnaire the entity survey adapted, sets such reports beside experiences without drugs. Anonymous and unpaid, it recruited through internet advertisements, email invitations and online social networks that it does not name (2014 to 2016; dates printed as 12/03/2014–08/01/2016) adults who reported an encounter with what they took to be God, a Higher Power, Ultimate Reality or an aspect or emissary of God (the purpose stated to everyone named these); each described their single most memorable encounter in one of two versions of the questionnaire, one for an encounter without any drug, by people who had never had one after a drug, and one for an encounter after a psychedelic. Of 12,725 who began, 1,702 did not meet the criteria, 5,165 did not finish (47% of the 11,023 who met them; editors' calculation) and 1,573 were excluded for other reasons (editors' sum), leaving 4,285: 809 without drugs and 3,476 after a psychedelic, of whom 606 after DMT other than ayahuasca (mostly smoked), 435 after ayahuasca, 1,184 after psilocybin and 1,251 after LSD. The no-drug group averaged 56.2 years of age and was 27% men, its experiences on average 20.5 years before the survey; the DMT group averaged 30.0 years and was 82% men, 4.7 years (the entity survey: 31.9 years, 77% men, about 4.6 years). Comparisons were adjusted for eight demographic factors but not for religion before the experience, which, as recalled, was Christian, Jewish or Islamic for 47% of the no-drug group and 7% of the DMT group. Shares of the no-drug group (809) and the DMT group (606), with the differences the authors call significant (p ≤ 0.001) marked: communication with what was encountered 63% and 80% (significant), two-way 22% and 28%; a message, task, mission or insight 78% and 74%; predictions about the future 21% and 21%; visual 48% and 83% (significant); best descriptor God 41% and 16% and Ultimate Reality 26% and 48% (both significant), Higher Power 15% and 25%; benevolent (kind, compassionate, altruistic) 86% and 75%; intelligent 80% and 87% (significant); malicious 1% and 8% (significant); existing at least partly in some other dimension or reality 68% and 76% (significant); continuing to exist after the encounter 74% and 53% (significant); among their five most personally meaningful experiences 74% and 81%, and among the five most psychologically challenging 32% and 47%; attributed change in well-being or life satisfaction, mean 2.38 and 2.26 (−3 to +3). Atheist identification, rated at the survey for before and after the encounter, fell from 3% to 1% in the no-drug group and from 25% to 7% in the DMT group; of those who recalled being atheist, 74% in the no-drug group and 67% across all psychedelic groups (about 24 and about 730 people; editors' arithmetic) no longer identified as atheist, a difference the authors found not significant. The entity survey reported its comparison with this DMT group only as significantly lower ratings of meaning, spiritual significance and lasting positive effects (t-tests, p < 0.001); the God-encounter DMT group's numbers against the entity survey's are personal meaning 6.97 against 6.3 and spiritual significance 7.14 against 6.5 (1 to 8), attributed well-being 2.26 against 2.0, and among the five most personally meaningful experiences 81% against 55%, spiritually significant 85% against 65% and psychologically challenging 47% against 32%; two-way communication was 28% against 40% (the entity survey's Discussion describes about 80% in both surveys as two-way communication, a figure that matches any communication, 80% and 84%), and the entity survey did not offer God, ultimate reality or higher power as labels, so the labels cannot be compared. The God-encounter authors say that the survey cannot tell whether the DMT group's differences from the psilocybin and LSD groups reflect the drug or expectation and context, and that popular beliefs about DMT entity encounters may have biased people who use DMT toward having them; their stated limitations are self-reports collected on average more than a decade later, possible social desirability, a long, unpaid, anonymous survey that could have selected the sample, unknown representativeness and 1% Black respondents, and they state that descriptive studies cannot settle whether God exists. The research was funded mainly by the Council on Spiritual Practices, whose convener was a co-author, and the Heffter Research Institute, on whose board the first author served, as the paper declares. As in the entity survey, these are reports and beliefs of people recruited because they had such an encounter: the survey cannot show how often such encounters happen, with or without drugs, or that a drug caused any feature or change. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team (two surveys from one group, sharing a questionnaire, so not independent).
plain: In a 2018 online survey, 2,561 adults who said they had met a 'being' after smoking or vaping DMT described their most memorable meeting, often years later. They most often called it a being, guide, spirit or alien, and about 1 in 7 an elf. Most said it seemed conscious, intelligent and kind, though 41 in 100 felt fear at some point; 72 in 100 believed it went on existing afterwards, and 69 in 100 said it gave them a message. 28 in 100 recalled being atheists before and 10 in 100 said they were atheists afterwards, but 'before' was remembered at the same time, years later. An earlier online survey by the same team asked people who said they had met 'God' to describe it, and people whose meeting happened without any drug told similar stories: of 809, 86 in 100 called it kind and 78 in 100 said it gave them a message, and the share calling themselves atheists fell too, though only from 3 to 1 in 100. The 606 in that survey who said they met 'God' after DMT (not as ayahuasca) more often said they saw it (83 against 48 in 100) and more often called it 'Ultimate Reality' than 'God'; 8 in 100 called it cruel, against 1 in 100 without drugs. Only people who said they had met a being or 'God' took part in either survey, so neither can show how often this happens, and these are their reports and beliefs, not facts about the beings.
population: 2,561 English-speaking adults recruited online (websites, forums and email; February to December 2018) who reported at least one encounter with a seemingly autonomous being or entity after a 'breakthrough' dose of smoked or vaporized DMT taken without other substances, excluding people with a psychotic disorder diagnosis; mean age 31.9; 77% men; 85% White; 64% living in the USA. For comparison, 4,285 English-speaking adults recruited online by the same group in 2014 to 2016 who reported an encounter with what they took to be God, a Higher Power, Ultimate Reality or an aspect or emissary of God: 809 whose encounter happened without any drug (mean age 56.2; 27% men) and 3,476 whose encounter followed a psychedelic, including 606 after DMT other than ayahuasca, mostly smoked (mean age 30.0; 82% men)
exposure: Smoked or vaporized DMT at a self-described 'breakthrough' dose (one with very strong effects), self-reported and untested; the single most memorable entity encounter, on average about 4.6 years before the survey (editors' calculation). In the comparison survey: the substance respondents believed they had taken before their most memorable God encounter, at a dose with moderate to strong effects (DMT other than ayahuasca, mostly smoked; ayahuasca; psilocybin; LSD), or no drug; on average 4.7 years before the survey in the DMT group and 20.5 years in the no-drug group
comparator: None within the entity survey (no group without an encounter or without DMT). In a separate survey by the same group, God encounters that happened without any drug (809 people, recruited into a separate version of the questionnaire and differing in age, sex and recalled religion) were compared with those after psychedelics, including 606 after DMT; neither survey included people without an encounter, and in both, religious identification 'before' was recalled in the same sitting as 'after'
outcome: Respondents' descriptions of the encounter (senses, communication, labels, emotions), their interpretation (how real it was, where the entity existed, its attributes, whether it continued to exist, change in their conception of reality, messages and predictions), religious identification recalled for before and reported for after, comparison with other life experiences, and lasting changes they attributed to it; in the comparison survey, the same kinds of items for God encounters with and without drugs, including the best descriptor of what was encountered (God, Ultimate Reality, Higher Power or an emissary of God)

evidence.locator: Method › Procedure; Method › Study recruitment flow, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Anonymous internet survey (hosted by Qualtrics) of people who said they had met what the study calls a seemingly autonomous being or entity after taking DMT; postings on websites (for example motherboard.com, facebook.com, reddit.com, dmt-nexus.me, bluelight.org and drugs-forum.com) and email announcements linked to it. At consent, people confirmed that they were 18 or older and fluent in English, had taken at least one 'breakthrough' dose of DMT (defined there as a dose with very strong psychoactive effects), and had met such a being or entity after DMT. The Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine review board approved the study. Recruitment ran from February to December 2018: 20,340 people clicked a link and 10,308 consented; 1129 were excluded at consent (150 had done the questionnaire before, 50 were under 18, 103 were not fluent in English, 342 had no breakthrough experience, 484 had met no entity); of the 9179 eligible, 4610 finished the survey and confirmed at the end that they believed their answers were accurate; 1839 of these were then excluded for an earlier psychotic disorder diagnosis (103), other substances that may have affected the DMT experience (1279), or DMT taken some way other than smoking or vaporizing (457). Potential harms: 1–5% attributed lasting negative changes to the experience; the authors then discuss potential harms that the survey did not examine: harmful outcomes may be undercounted, since people whose lives had been seriously disrupted may have been less inclined to take part and each person described only the most memorable experience; the shifts in religious identification and worldview could be judged good by some and bad by others, and changed beliefs might lead to physical, psychological or epistemic harm; the authors say the study provided no evidence of such harmful outcomes and that future studies should ask whether such beliefs lead to self-destructive behaviour or mark the start of a psychotic disorder. Limitations: bias from looking back and from wanting to give acceptable answers; a single cross-sectional assessment, which the authors say rules out any causal interpretation and cannot show whether the sample represents people who use DMT; exclusions for other substances, changa and routes other than vaporizing or smoking; reports limited to the most memorable experience; how common such encounters are among people who use DMT, and how reliably they recur, are left to future studies. Endorsement was compared with general linear models adjusted for eight dichotomous covariates (age at the survey over 32, age at the experience over 23, sex, White race, college graduate, US resident, income over $50K a year, ever married) and called significant at p ≤ 0.001; before–after religious orientation was compared with z-tests of dependent proportions at Bonferroni-adjusted p ≤ 0.05. evidence.extracted: The DMT Group differed from the Psilocybin and LSD groups on 16 of 76 items; the authors state that the survey cannot distinguish whether these differences reflect true pharmacological differences or differences in expectancy and context, and consider it plausible that popular beliefs about DMT, with special interest in DMT entity encounters, may have biased people who use DMT toward having such experiences. They call it an interesting finding that in the Non-Drug Group and each psychedelic group most of those who identified as atheist before no longer did afterwards, and name prospective research on changes in religious orientation as an important future direction. Their summary that about one-third rated the experience among the 5 most psychologically challenging of their lives, and about 15% the single most, is given without group figures. While acknowledging both similarities and differences between the Non-Drug and Psychedelic groups, they call the descriptive details, interpretation and consequences markedly similar, as the most robust general pattern across a wide range of questions; they suggest that the preference for God or for Ultimate Reality may reflect semantics and interpretation, and state that descriptive studies, however detailed, cannot definitively address claims about the existence of God. Limitations: self-reports collected retrospectively, often years later (on average over a decade), raising concern that memories may have changed over time; social desirability or other implicit biases, for example participants may have answered affirmatively more readily because they believed, rightly or not, that the researchers wanted such answers; a time-consuming (averaging 50 minutes), uncompensated and anonymous survey that could have contributed to selection bias; unknown representativeness of the larger populations who may have had such experiences; and only 1% Black or African-American in both groups.

risk_of_bias.note: Measurement (card sc_davis_2020b, JBI prevalence checklist, high): a study-specific questionnaire without validation; one report of the single most memorable encounter, on average about 4.6 years earlier (editors' calculation); 'before' religious identification recalled in the same sitting as 'after'; lasting changes are respondents' attributions, not measured change; half of the eligible people who consented did not complete (4,610 of 9,179 did), and those who did not are not described; item non-response is not reported; open-ended answers were coded by the authors (94% to 95% agreement on a 20% subsample). The God-encounter survey (card sc_griffiths_2019, JBI prevalence checklist, high) has the same kinds of problems: study-made items without reported validation; the single most memorable encounter recalled on average 11.0 years later (20.5 years in the no-drug group); religion 'before' rated at the survey; attributed rather than measured change; and 5,165 of the 11,023 who met its criteria did not finish (47%, editors' calculation) and are not described.

inconsistency.note: Not rated down. Where the two surveys asked the same questions about DMT experiences, the answers point the same way (communication 84% and 80%; a message 69% and 74%; predictions 19% and 21%; atheist identification falling from 28% to 10% and from 25% to 7%), while some shares differ (two-way communication 40% and 28%; continued to exist 72% and 53%; among the five most personally meaningful experiences 55% and 81%), plausibly because one survey sampled entity encounters and the other encounters taken to be God or Ultimate Reality; each sample is described separately and nothing is pooled.

indirectness.note: Coverage: only people who reported an encounter could take part, recruited mainly through DMT and drug websites, in English; 2,049 completers were excluded (psychotic disorder, other substances, other routes, changa, data quality), and each described only the most memorable encounter. The shares describe this filtered group, not people who use DMT, not all encounters, and not experiences with ayahuasca or DMT taken another way. The God-encounter survey required an encounter that people took to be God, a Higher Power, Ultimate Reality or an aspect or emissary of God, named in the purpose given to everyone; it does not name its recruitment sources, and its no-drug and psychedelic groups were recruited into separate versions of the questionnaire and differ in age, sex and recalled religion. Its shares describe those groups, and its DMT group's encounters were selected as God encounters, not entity encounters as such.

imprecision.note: Not rated down: 2,561 respondents give shares precise to about plus or minus 2 percentage points, and the God-encounter survey's groups of 809 and 606 to about 3 to 4 points (editors' calculations); its no-drug share of former atheists who no longer identified as atheist rests on about 24 people (editors' arithmetic) and is imprecise, but nothing here rests on that share alone.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for two surveys from one group.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the population sampled (METHODS §6.3): starts low; down one for measurement (risk of bias) and one for coverage (indirectness), giving very low, the floor; never upgraded. 'Describes' because it reports what respondents said they experienced and believed; it makes no claim that the beings exist, that the messages or predictions are true, or that the experience caused the changes in belief or well-being that respondents attributed to it, which a single cross-sectional report cannot show, as its authors state. The abstract's conclusion that aspects of the experience produced profound and enduring changes in worldview is not adopted as a causal finding, and the suggestion that DMT could help in therapy was not tested. Companion papers of 12 November: the authors' earlier God-encounter survey (Griffiths et al., 2019; card sc_griffiths_2019, JBI prevalence checklist, high), read in full, supplies the comparison that the entity survey reported only as t-tests (p < 0.001), with each group's numbers and denominators, and a group whose encounters happened without any drug: a communicating, intelligent, mostly benevolent presence, messages and a fall in recalled atheist identification are reported without drugs too, so these kinds of report are not specific to DMT. Its recruitment cannot represent how often such encounters happen, people who would not answer a long English online survey whose stated purpose named God, or typical rather than most memorable experiences; its group differences are descriptive, because the groups were recruited into separate versions and differ in age, sex and recalled religion before the experience (not adjusted), and its authors say it cannot separate DMT's pharmacology from expectation and context. It shares the entity survey's limits, so the rating stays very low. Status replicated by the same team: where the two surveys asked the same questions about DMT experiences the answers point the same way, but the surveys share investigators, a questionnaire and online recruitment, so they are not independent replication (METHODS §6.3, overlapping evidence); the labels (being, guide, spirit, alien, elf) rest on the entity survey alone. Published descriptions of experiences without drugs, which the entity survey cites, are still not used. The breakthrough criterion and the route are reported as study conditions only.
